claims.text: The superior corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a chromium-enriched passive oxide film.
The chromium-enriched passive oxide film forms in situ and remains stable under service conditions.
Chromium in steel preferentially oxidizes under service conditions.
Preferential chromium oxidation produces a compact, adherent passive film.
A compact passive film limits ion transport and slows corrosion-reaction kinetics.
Steels containing sufficient chromium retain a stable passive film over extended exposure.
Steels with lower chromium content fail to form an effective passive barrier.
Failure to form an effective passive barrier causes accelerated corrosion in lower-chromium steels.
Higher-chromium steels will form passive films faster than lower-chromium baseline steels.
Higher-chromium steels will develop more compact and more stable passive films with higher polarization resistance.
Higher-chromium steels will have significantly lower corrosion rates than lower-chromium steels under otherwise identical conditions.
Passive-film degradation or failure will correlate with increased corrosion rates.
Standard low-chromium steels form less robust passive films and exhibit higher corrosion rates.
The proposed mechanism should operate in acidic, basic, and saline media at moderate-to-high temperatures and radiation levels typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
Extreme conditions may hinder passive-film formation or allow microstructural factors to dominate corrosion behavior.
Grain-boundary effects, precipitates, and alloy segregation may contribute to corrosion resistance under extreme irradiation.
Electrochemical impedance measurements can provide indicators of passive-film resistance, surface heterogeneity, and compactness.

A failure of high-chromium samples to show statistically significant improvements in both passive-film characteristics and corrosion rate relative to the low-chromium control would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
